title: Land Value Tax Enables Green Growth (Forrester, EJPE 19(1), 2026)
what_was_fetched: f1_forrester_green_growth.pdf (full text, 23 PDF pages, CC BY 4.0, downloaded from https://ejpe.org/journal/article/download/1038/799 via plain curl with browser UA); text in f1_forrester_green_growth.txt (layout), f1_paged.txt (page-tagged '[pN]' lines), f1_forrester_dehyph.txt (hyphenation removed, '[[PDF pN]]' markers; best for grep).
f1_landing.html / f1_landing.txt (OJS landing page: affiliation, abstract, issue, licence).
f1_about.txt and f1_subm.txt (EJPE About and Submissions pages: peer-review policy).
verdict: NEW research/forrester-lvt-green-growth.md (title style: 'Land Value Tax Enables Green Growth (Forrester, 2026)'; tier: important). Not an ENRICH of research/forrester-property-rights-natural-resources.md: different paper, different question (applied environmental/growth argument vs. Locke/Nozick original-acquisition theory), although the new paper cites the older one at PDF p.8 ('Forrester 2026; Layman 2020') for the deontological ground and lists it in references (PDF p.21). Then ENRICH (small, link-in) the pages below so the new page has >=2 inbound links. (1) concepts/ecological-georgism.md: insert a new H2 '## Growth, Degrowth and Green Growth' immediately after the '## The Argument' section's last paragraph and before '## Significance' (the page currently has Daly's steady-state throughput argument only under 'Book Findings' and no response from the Georgist side to degrowth). One paragraph: Forrester argues the growth-environment conflict is contingent on private ownership, LVT plus severance taxes correct underuse of land / overuse of depletables; label it a philosophical argument by one author, peer-reviewed, no empirical test. (2) concepts/resource-rents.md: insert one sentence at the end of '## Capturing Resource Rent' (after the sentence ending '...carries little deadweight loss.') distinguishing annual-rent capture for land from severance tax for depletables (PDF p.13: annual tax on a deposit would speed extraction), linking to the new page. (3) concepts/deadweight-loss.md: add one sentence to '## Why Land Value Tax Has Zero Deadweight Loss' after the paragraph ending 'Milton Friedman to the authors of the Mirrlees Review.' noting the 2026 philosophical restatement (fixed-supply argument; PDF p.7) and its claim that shifting the base 'reclaims the deadweight loss of taxation' on labour and capital (PDF p.18) - only if T1 judges it adds something beyond the Smith/Pigou/Friedman material already there; otherwise just a See Also link. (4) benefits/lvt-reduces-sprawl.md: See Also link only (Forrester's III.1 densification/green-city argument, PDF pp.10-13, leans on Glaeser & Kahn 2010, Hsieh & Moretti 2019, Duranton & Puga 2023 which the wiki may already hold; research/duranton-puga-urban-growth exists). (5) research/forrester-property-rights-natural-resources.md: add the new page to See Also and one clause in the opening Summary noting the companion paper. (6) Optional: guides/portal-climate-and-commons.md '## Resource rents - the most conditional case' link. No severance-tax concept page or degrowth page exists in the wiki (checked digest and concepts/); the nearest homes are ecological-georgism, resource-rents and research/gaffney-california-severance-tax. A new concepts/degrowth stub is NOT recommended on this one source.
claim_grade: B (peer-reviewed normative/analytic argument; the empirical claims it leans on are relayed from other scholars, not tested here). Source tier per EDITORIAL 4c: Tier 1 for use as an academic philosophy-of-economics argument (peer-reviewed article in a double-blind peer-reviewed journal, author a university academic; Forrester is not in sources/audit/people-tiers.json, so judged by rubric: recognised-scholar-in-a-peer-reviewed-venue = Tier 1 for 'Forrester argues'; but it is a single new paper and should be written as 'argues', not as established support for green-growth empirics). The paper contains no original data, estimates or model; do not grade any of its empirical sentences above C/D on Forrester's say-so (e.g. 'one barrel of oil buys more than twice as much GDP today as in the 1970s' is relayed from a World Bank blog, PDF p.4 and fn.4).
content_summary: Bibliographic: Paul Forrester, 'Land Value Tax Enables Green Growth', Erasmus Journal for Philosophy and Economics 19(1), Summer 2026, published 2026-10-12, DOI 10.23941/ejpe.v19i1.1038, page numbers 'aa-aa' (First View; cite PDF pages). Section: 'Special Issue on Degrowth' within 'Vol. 19 No. 1 (2026): Summer 2026 (Special Issue on the 250th Anniversary of The Wealth of Nations) (First View)'. JEL O44, Q24, Q38, D63. CC BY 4.0. [f1_landing.txt: 'Published 2026-10-12'; f1_forrester_dehyph.txt PDF p.1: 'JEL Classification: O44; Q24; Q38; D63']

Affiliation as stated on the paper: 'Wharton Business School, University of Pennsylvania' (PDF p.1 and OJS citation_author_institution; grep 'Wharton Business School' in f1_landing.txt / f1_paged.txt).

Peer-review status: EJPE describes itself as 'a peer-reviewed bi-annual academic journal supported by the Erasmus Institute for Philosophy and Economics at the Erasmus School of Philosophy of Erasmus University Rotterdam'; 'All accepted submissions are anonymously double-blind peer-reviewed by a minimum of two experts' [f1_about.txt]. Internal evidence the paper went through review: fn.7 (PDF p.5) 'like an anonymous reviewer does'. Caveat: issue is marked '(First View)', i.e. online-first before final pagination; special issue (guest-edited, topic: degrowth).

CONTINGENCY THESIS (abstract, PDF p.1): "the conflict between growth and the environment is contingent on the private ownership of natural resources." Body (PDF p.3): "the inconsistency between such reductions and economic growth is not necessary, but rather is contingent upon our failure to adopt just institutions for the governance and ownership of natural resources." Grep: 'contingent on the private ownership' and 'contingent upon our failure' in f1_forrester_dehyph.txt.

UNDERUSE vs OVERUSE (PDF p.10, III intro): "Under a regime of private ownership, inexhaustible resources tend to be underused, and exhaustible resources tend to be overused." Remedy as stated there: for land, tax must "collect the rental value of the resource in each period, which prevents speculative underuse"; for depletables, collect the unimproved value "when the resource is developed, preventing premature overuse". Grep 'tend to be underused'.

NO-DEADWEIGHT-LOSS CLAIM: abstract (PDF p.1) "Natural resources are the ideal tax base because they do not cause deadweight loss." Argument (PDF p.7, II): "A tax on any good that has a perfectly inelastic supply does not cause deadweight loss, because the supply of the good does not change in response to the tax." Same page: LVT "garners wide support from economists, even otherwise anti-tax libertarian economists like Milton Friedman who regard it as 'the least bad tax'" (Friedman quote is unreferenced in the paper). Grep 'perfectly inelastic supply' and 'the least bad tax'. Tension to flag for T1: on PDF p.13 the paper says an annual tax on an oil deposit would make the owner extract sooner, which is why severance (extraction-time) taxes are used and are meant to change timing ("to incentivize the owner to delay the extraction"); so the zero-deadweight-loss premise is stated for fixed-supply land/oil in situ, while the severance tax is designed to alter behaviour. Also PDF p.18: shifting the base "would also accelerate growth by reclaiming the deadweight loss of taxation that is associated with taxes on labor and capital."

SYMMETRICAL PRE-POLITICAL ENTITLEMENTS (PDF p.8, II): "Since no one made natural resources, no one in particular is entitled to them; rather, all people have symmetrical entitlements to natural resources." And (PDF p.7) the classical-to-George view that "people are symmetrically entitled to natural resources, and as such the public should appropriate the value of natural resources, while people are differentially entitled to labor and capital". Grep 'symmetrical entitlements to natural resources'. The deontological/republican grounds cite 'Forrester 2026; Layman 2020' (PDF p.8); utilitarian ground cites 'Jacobson (forthcoming)' (fn.9).

LVT-NOT-DEGROWTH CONCLUSION: abstract (PDF p.1) "Land value tax, not degrowth, should be the cornerstone of a green new deal." Body (PDF p.3): "public appropriation of natural resource value is the best, and perhaps the only, way to address the environmental crisis without sacrificing growth." Conclusion (PDF p.20): "Our aim should not be to shrink the economy, but rather, it should be to embrace and maximize the human side of the economy that adds value to natural resources". Grep 'not degrowth, should be the cornerstone', 'perhaps the only', 'shrink the economy'. Note the hedge on PDF p.9: public appropriation is "neither strictly necessary ... nor ... sufficient" for green growth.

Mechanism for land (PDF pp.10-13, III.1): most land value is in cities; private ownership of urban land plus homeowner-lobbied land-use rules (setbacks, single-family zoning, FARs, height limits) cause underuse; an LVT with buildings untaxed and most or all land value publicly appropriated would 'cause a development boom in the central locations' and raise carrying cost of idle land (PDF pp.12-13). Fn.13 (PDF pp.11-12): under LVT homeowners 'would own their buildings but not their land, and as such would not have an incentive to lobby for restrictive land use regulations' - an argument, untested here. Empirical premises are relayed: Hsieh & Moretti 2019 and Duranton & Puga 2023 on spatial misallocation (PDF p.11), Glaeser & Kahn 2010 on California regulation pushing growth to higher-emission inland places (PDF p.12), Jones & Kammen 2014 on suburban footprints (PDF p.11).

Mechanism for depletables (PDF pp.13-17, III.2): severance tax on in-situ value (value of finished resource minus all improvements, PDF pp.13-14), set on a fair-share-for-future-generations logic; Forrester says he 'cannot provide a full model with an analytical solution' (PDF p.15). Severance taxes 'go above and beyond' a Pigouvian carbon tax, which he supports as well (PDF p.16). Fn.17 (PDF p.15): private ownership plus severance tax likely better than direct public ownership for most countries (short-termism; resource curse, citing Wenar 2015).

Jevons paradox (PDF pp.17-20, III.3): the paper's main theoretical novelty - a tax that tracks the unimproved value of a resource rises when efficiency gains raise demand, so 'the price reduction for the resource is offset by a tax increase on the unimproved resource' (spans the PDF p.19/p.20 break; grep 'reduction for the resource is offset' in f1_forrester_dehyph.txt) and the Jevons rebound 'dissolves'. This is asserted, not modelled or tested.
existing_wiki_coverage: Corpus digest and repo grep ('degrowth', 'green growth', 'Jevons', 'severance', 'decoupl', 'ejpe', 'Erasmus Journal'): no wiki page covers degrowth or green growth; 'degrowth' appears only in research/tornberg-anti-growth-machine.md (Tornberg distinguishes his 'anti-growth machine' from degrowth politics). concepts/ecological-georgism.md (last_reviewed 2026-07-18) carries the Georgist-ecological extension (carbon, severance, pollution) and Daly's steady-state throughput argument under '## Book Findings', but nothing responds to degrowth. concepts/resource-rents.md covers severance tax design (Gaffney sections, research/gaffney-california-severance-tax). concepts/deadweight-loss.md '## Why Land Value Tax Has Zero Deadweight Loss' already has Smith 1776, Pigou 1920, Friedman, Mirrlees; Forrester adds nothing new on the theory. benefits/lvt-reduces-sprawl.md and research/duranton-puga-urban-growth.md cover the densification premise. research/forrester-property-rights-natural-resources.md exists (abstract-only page, last_reviewed 2026-08-27, inbound from objections/lvt-is-socialism.md and people/john-locke.md) - the new page should link to it. EJPE/Forrester DOI not in repo (grep). Forrester is not in sources/audit/people-tiers.json.
uncertainties: Single-author normative paper in a special issue; no empirical test of the central claim that LVT yields absolute decoupling. Write as 'Forrester argues', and keep any 'LVT enables green growth' headline off concept pages as a finding.
Forrester's Wharton unit is not named on the paper (only 'Wharton Business School, University of Pennsylvania'); do not add a department or rank.

The paper's own claims that Friedman called LVT 'the least bad tax' is unreferenced in the paper; the wiki already has a Friedman's Endorsement section on concepts/land-value-tax.md, cite that, not Forrester, for the Friedman point.

Tension noted above between the zero-deadweight-loss premise and severance taxes deliberately shifting extraction timing (PDF p.7 vs p.13); T1 should decide whether to carry the abstract's 'no deadweight loss' wording or the more careful p.7 'perfectly inelastic supply' wording.
Cites two forthcoming works by collaborator Martin Jacobson (Social Theory and Practice; Philosophy of the Social Sciences) that are not yet retrievable; any page link to them would be premature.
Page numbers: the journal gives 'aa-aa'; every locator in this brief is the PDF page (1-23), which equals the EJPE galley page. Re-check if the final pagination is assigned.
Peer-review status: EJPE policy is double-blind; this article is 'First View' in a guest-edited special issue; fn.7 confirms an anonymous reviewer. No review report or editor note was seen.

title: LoGRI Property Tax Diagnostic Toolkit (Prichard, 2026) - Summary (Policy Brief 15) and full Guidance Note 05
what_was_fetched: f2_logri_landing.html / f2_logri_landing.txt (LoGRI landing page, 29 September 2026, citation, keywords, funder logos).

f2_toolkit_full.pdf (the PDF at the queue's utoronto.scholaris.ca bitstream 2900c048-..., 26 pages; this is the FULL 'Guidance Note 05 | August 2026'); text in f2_toolkit_full.txt and f2_toolkit_paged.txt ('[pN]' tags; printed page = PDF page).

f2_summary_PB15.pdf (the 9-page 'Policy Brief 15 | September 2026' executive summary, bitstream c1339776-9773-4ad7-b0f1-d36f6bb8b4db, found via the TSpace item page f2_scholaris_item.html / f2_scholaris_item_jina.txt, https://utoronto.scholaris.ca/items/1cd92605-d4d8-4212-afa2-66a6b16eda15); text in f2_summary_PB15_paged.txt.

Note: the queue's 'full guidance note' bitstream is the 26-page toolkit; the landing page's own 'PDF (English)' is the 9-page summary. Both saved. Everything fetched with plain curl/browser UA; nothing blocked.
verdict: ENRICH (light, low priority) research/franzsen-mccluskey-property-tax-africa.md; no NEW page; REJECT as a standalone research page. Reason: the toolkit is a diagnostic how-to (technical assessment, political-economy assessment, binding constraints, recommendations) with no empirical findings, no named-country results and exactly one unsourced aggregate (property tax below 0.2% of GDP in most lower-income countries, p.7). It says nothing about land-value or site-value bases, nothing about LVT, and treats area-based valuation only as one option in a list. Insertion point: research/franzsen-mccluskey-property-tax-africa.md, section '## Nuances and Limits', as a new final bullet after the bullet beginning '**Institutional perspective.**': 'A 2026 diagnostic framework from the Local Government Revenue Initiative (University of Toronto) breaks the property tax cycle into identification, valuation, rates and exemptions, billing, appeals, payments, voluntary compliance and enforcement, and stresses that underperformance is often political and administrative rather than technical, consistent with this book's finding that coverage, valuation and collection, not the statutory rate, are binding (Prichard 2026, pp.7, 11-18).' plus a See Also entry '- [LoGRI Property Tax Diagnostic Toolkit (Prichard, 2026)](...)' only if T1 wants it linkable; since no page is created, cite in Sources as entry 4: 'Wilson Prichard (2026), LoGRI Property Tax Diagnostic Toolkit, Guidance Note 05 (Aug 2026) and Policy Brief 15 (Sep 2026), University of Toronto; https://logri.org/publication/logri-property-tax-diagnostic-toolkit-summary/ - used for the property-tax-cycle framework and the sub-0.2%-of-GDP lower-income-country figure (B-claim; figure unsourced in the toolkit)'. Optional second touch: concepts/mass-appraisal-methods.md '## Limits and Open Questions' one sentence that, in lower-income-country diagnostics, valuation is one stage of a cycle and approaches range from self-declaration and area-based to points-based and model-driven CAMA (Prichard 2026, p.14) - add only if T1 wants a LIC counterpoint; objections/land-cannot-be-assessed.md and research/brockmeyer-property-tax-developing.md and research/bergeron-tourek-weigel-drc-property-tax.md need no change (the toolkit adds no causal or valuation evidence beyond them). If T1 prefers to skip, REJECT is defensible; do not spend a NEW page on it.
claim_grade: B for the framework description (primary document, accurately summarised from the author's own text); C for the 'below 0.2% of GDP' aggregate (stated without citation in the toolkit, p.7). Source tier per EDITORIAL 4c: Tier 1 - Wilson Prichard is a University of Toronto (Munk School) professor and Chair of LoGRI with three monographs (2015, 2018, 2022) per the toolkit's author note (f2_toolkit_paged.txt p.4); LoGRI is an institutional research initiative of the Munk School, publisher University of Toronto, CC BY 4.0, funder logos on the landing page include the Gates Foundation. Neither 'Prichard', 'Wilson Prichard' nor 'LoGRI' is in sources/audit/people-tiers.json (grep checked; only 'Lincoln Institute' appears, in tier1_confirmed). PROPOSED: add both 'Wilson Prichard' and 'LoGRI / Local Government Revenue Initiative (University of Toronto Munk School)' to tier1_confirmed, with the note 'diagnostic and policy-guidance material carried as the initiative's own method, not as causal evidence'.
content_summary: Document identity: 'LoGRI Property Tax Diagnostic Toolkit', Wilson Prichard, 'GUIDANCE NOTE 05 | AUGUST 2026', University of Toronto, CC BY 4.0 [f2_toolkit_paged.txt p.1, p.3]. Executive summary: 'POLICY BRIEF 15 | SEPTEMBER 2026' [f2_summary_PB15_paged.txt p.1]; landing page date 29 September 2026; citation 'Prichard, Wilson. (2026). "LoGRI Property Tax Diagnostic Toolkit." Policy Brief 15. University of Toronto: Local Government Revenue Initiative.' [f2_logri_landing.txt]. Keywords on landing: 'property tax reform, diagnostic assessment, political economy, binding constraints'.

ONLY FIGURES (p.7, f2_toolkit_paged.txt, repeated in summary p.1 without the numbers): "Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries frequently collect between 1 per cent and 2 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) in property tax revenues" and "collection in most countries appears to be less than 0.2 per cent of GDP. This makes property tax the most underperforming major tax across lower-income countries." Neither number carries a citation or year in the toolkit. No collection rates, no country examples, no named case studies anywhere in the 26 pages (grep for Kenya, Rwanda, Ghana, Sierra Leone, Freetown, Uganda, Tanzania, DRC etc. returns nothing; only 'Georgia State University' in a footnote).
Experience base (p.7): the approach "reflects experience from conducting diagnostic assessments in more than a dozen countries"; an early version dates to 2018-19 (p.6 Acknowledgements).

Framework (pp.8-25): four components - technical assessment (11 functions: overall performance, property identification, valuation, rates and exemptions, billing, appeals, payments, voluntary compliance, enforcement, digital systems, human resources/financing), political economy assessment (political leadership, administrative leadership, inter-institutional cooperation, taxpayer support), binding constraints analysis, reform recommendations. Five principles: holistic, multidisciplinary, administrative detail, diagnostics and prioritisation, locally appropriate solutions (p.7). Frames itself as 'a corrective to more prescriptive "best-practice"-driven approaches' (p.8). Reform strategy 'may be "second best"' (summary p.6).

Performance model (p.11): follows Kelly (2013) and Kelly, White & Anand (2020, World Bank 'Property tax diagnostic manual'): potential = tax base x rate, realised through coverage ratio (CVR), valuation ratio (VR), tax levy ratio (TLR) and collection ratio (CLR). The toolkit does not report values for these ratios.

VALUATION BASES (p.14, section 3.3): lists "self-declaration, area-based approaches, expert valuation approaches, and systems of computer assisted mass appraisal", with CAMA from "points-based valuation to more complex model-driven approaches", and asks whether the system seeks "market value (e.g. sales value, rental value)" or non-market-value bases "(e.g. area-based or adjusted area-based systems)", for "built and unbuilt properties". It does NOT discuss land-value, site-value or unimproved-value bases, land/improvement separation, or LVT; grep for 'site value', 'land value', 'unimproved', 'split rate' returns nothing. 'Land' appears only in land registration/titling (pp.13, 22). Unbuilt properties are mentioned as a billing/enforcement difficulty (p.18: 'identifying owners and levying penalties may be especially difficult').

Enforcement (p.18): "Many governments report large uncollected property tax arrears, often due to a combination of poor tracking systems, weak penalties, and political reluctance to enforce property tax laws." (unquantified).

Authorship: author note p.4 of the full note says 'Associate Professor at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, and Department of Political Science, a Research Fellow at the Institute of Development Studies (IDS), and Chair of the LoGRI program'; the September summary p.7 says 'Professor'. Does not mention ICTD in the document (the queue context's 'ICTD' is not on the page).
existing_wiki_coverage: Zero repo hits for 'logri' or 'prichard' (grep over .md/.csv/.json outside scratchpad/LOOPLOG/queue). research/franzsen-mccluskey-property-tax-africa.md (last_reviewed 2026-07-12; Lincoln Institute 2017 volume) already carries: effective property-tax yield about 0.3% of GDP across African countries (ch.36), valuation 'one of the weakest links', collection rates as low as 20% (Niamey 2007), under 50% (Lusaka 2011), under 70% (Dar es Salaam 2006-11), formally registered land under 1% of parcels in Cameroon and Rwanda, area-based valuation as pragmatic second best. Its See Also states India's take is under 0.2% of GDP. research/brockmeyer-property-tax-developing.md (Mexico natural experiments: rate increases raise welfare, aggressive enforcement double-edged) and research/bergeron-tourek-weigel-drc-property-tax.md (Kananga, 38,028 owners; status quo rate above revenue-maximising rate; enforcement lifts the ceiling) carry the causal evidence the toolkit lacks. concepts/mass-appraisal-methods.md (hedonic, CAMA, Shapley; 'Existing Practice at Scale' Estonia/Denmark/Australia) and objections/land-cannot-be-assessed.md (Estonia, Denmark, FHFA land data; Limits and Caveats section) are about land/improvement separation in high-capacity jurisdictions - the toolkit does not engage with that. Other related pages in digest: research/almy-oecd-valuation-assessment, research/kakumu-kenya-site-value-tax, places/nigeria, events/telangana-cure-bill-hyderabad, research/duflo-hanna-olken-tandon-chennai-outsourcing.
uncertainties: The sub-0.2%-of-GDP figure is unsourced and conflicts in scope (not in value) with the wiki's 0.3% African average from Franzsen & McCluskey (2017): do not average or reconcile them in prose; attribute each to its source and scope (the toolkit speaks of 'most' lower-income countries, 'appears to be').

Prichard's title differs between documents (Associate Professor in the August full note; Professor in the September summary); safest wording is 'Chair of LoGRI at the University of Toronto's Munk School'. The queue context mentions ICTD; the documents do not.

Funding: landing page includes funder logos (Gates Foundation file present in the page source); a donor-funded policy-guidance document. Treat as institutional method statement, not independent evaluation.
The toolkit is explicitly not an LVT document; any Georgist framing on a page would be the wiki's inference and should be avoided or flagged as such.
The 'verified 200' PDF in the queue is the 26-page full note, not the summary; the summary PDF has a separate bitstream (c1339776-...).

ALSO ENRICH concepts/speculative-vacancy.md: append one bullet at the end of '## Limits and Caveats' (after the bullet ending '...not emptiness counts alone.') titled along the lines of 'Vacancy and dereliction charges depend on enforcement design', linking to the Ireland section and to research/segu-vacancy-tax-france.md and research/vancouver-empty-homes-tax.md; and add a See Also link on problems/speculative-vacancy-wastes-cities.md (its '## Counter-Evidence' or '## See Also'). No NEW research page: the campaigners' essay is Tier 2 and the evidence belongs to the government/statistical primaries; a NEW places/ireland-vacancy... is not needed. WAIT for Part 2 (due Thu 22 Oct 2026) before describing the design flaws of the new tax; Part 1 covers history and the levy only. Framing note for T1: the Derelict Sites Levy and the Derelict Property Tax are status-based penalty charges (7% of market value for registered derelict urban land), not land value taxes; link them to the wiki's vacancy-tax material as holding-cost charges on idle property, and say so, rather than implying they are Georgist LVT.

content_summary: CLAIM-BY-CLAIM TRACE (authors' claim -> primary check; all in saved files):

(1) '3% levy (increased to 7% in 2020)': VERIFIED A, with a date correction. Revised Act s.23(3): 3 per cent for the first prescribed year and subsequent years 'falling before the year 2020'; '(c) in respect of the local financial year 2020 or any subsequent local financial year ... 7 per cent of the said market value' - substituted '(19.07.2018) by Planning and Development (Amendment) Act 2018 (16/2018), s. 59, commenced on enactment'. So the 7% was legislated in July 2018 and applies from local financial year 2020. Levy commenced by S.I. No. 286 of 1991 (20.11.1991) [f3_derelict_sites_act_1990_revised.txt, grep '7 per cent of the said market value', 'Planning and Development (Amendment) Act 2018']. Other statutory facts: levy applies to 'urban land in relation to which a market value has been determined and stands entered on the register on the first day of January' (s.23(1)); register is kept by each local authority (s.8(1)); an authority may remove an entry (s.8(3)); simple interest at 1.25 per cent per month on unpaid levy (s.23(8)); levy is not payable where the Urban Regeneration and Housing Act 2015 vacant site levy applies (s.23(1A)). Gov.ie page states the same: 'Charge owners a Derelict Site Levy of 7% of the property's market value each year' [f3_gov_dpt_page.txt].

(2) 'only 2,140 derelict properties registered at the end of 2024': VERIFIED A. gov.ie spreadsheet total row: 'No. of Derelict Sites on Register at 31 December 2024' = 2,140 (1,916 at 1 Jan 2024; 563 entered; 339 removed) [f3_gov_2024_Derelict_Sites_Statistics.txt, grep 'Total\t2869'; also f3_gov_dpt_page.txt 'At the end of 2024, there were 2,140 sites']. NB the register counts SITES (residential and commercial), not 'homes'.

(3) '19,821 derelict homes counted by Geodirectory in Q2 2025': VERIFIED B. '19,821 residential buildings were classified as derelict in June 2025, 2.9% lower compared to June 2024' [f3_geodir_q2_2025_news.txt; EY report f3_geodirectory_ey_q2_2025.txt: 'total of 19,821 derelict units']. GeoDirectory definition: 'A building is classified as derelict when structural work/reconstruction is needed before it can be re-occupied, usually leaving the building dormant for several years' (EY report footnote). Q4 2025 (Dec 2025): 19,438 derelict units, down 3.3% [f3_geodir_q4_2025_news.txt].

(4) '90% of derelict homes are not even officially registered': authors' ARITHMETIC, not a published statistic: 1 - 2,140/19,821 = 89.2%. Mixes dates (Dec 2024 vs June 2025) and universes (register: all derelict sites incl. commercial and non-dwelling land; GeoDirectory: residential address points only). Present as 'roughly nine in ten on the campaigners' comparison'. The same authors made the same comparison in 2021: 'With just 1,548 properties currently on all derelict site registers, it represents 6.8% of the derelict homes identified by Geodirectory (22,754)' [f3_oireachtas_anois_opening_statement_2021-12-14.txt].

(5) 'only 36% of registered derelict sites were invoiced (778 out of 2,140)': VERIFIED A (arithmetic 778/2,140 = 36.4%). Spreadsheet column 'No. of Derelict Sites levied during the year' total = 778; 'Amount levied during the year' total = EUR 8,593,892. Note 778 sites levied in the year vs 2,140 on the register at year end.

(6) '10 councils didn't even bother invoicing any owners': NOT MATCHED - primary shows 9 authorities with zero sites levied in 2024: Cavan, Donegal, Fingal, Galway City, Galway County, Kerry, Leitrim, Longford, Monaghan. Different count: 11 of 31 authorities received NO levy payments at all in 2024 (zero in 'Total Amount received in respect of levies in 2024': Cavan, Donegal, Fingal, Galway City, Galway County, Leitrim, Longford, Monaghan, Tipperary, Westmeath, Wicklow; Kerry levied nothing but received EUR 17,920 on older levies) - matches Irish Examiner 16 Jun 2026 ('11 of Ireland's 31 local authorities collected no levies at all in 2024') [f3_irishexaminer_revenue_wont_collect.txt]. Use the primary: 9 authorities levied nothing; 11 collected nothing.

(7) 'Cork City Council wrote off EUR 3.7m ... more than the EUR 3.2m they collected over the same period': VERIFIED B (council figures reported by Irish Examiner): 2016-2025 almost EUR 12m invoiced across 651 sites, EUR 3.25m paid, EUR 3.67m written off across 99 sites [f3_irishexaminer_cork_writeoff.txt]. IMPORTANT NUANCE the essay omits: 'Of the total write-offs implemented since 2016, 79% were due to dereliction being removed by the property owner or the property being acquired by council'; only 8% were deemed 'uncollectable'. Also Cork City 2024 primary row: 92 sites levied, EUR 2,065,637 levied, EUR 477,604 total received, EUR 5,929,707 outstanding at 31 Dec 2024.

(8) 'less than 10% of Derelict Sites Levies invoiced nationwide were actually paid in 2024': VERIFIED A by computation: 'Amount received in respect of sites levied during 2024' EUR 819,556 / 'Amount levied during the year' EUR 8,593,892 = 9.5%. Total received in 2024 on all years' levies = EUR 2,181,761 = 25.4% of the 2024 amount levied (a different, non-comparable ratio). State which ratio is used.

(9) 'EUR 42m worth of Derelict Sites Levies outstanding': NOT VERIFIED. The Department's 2024 return gives 'Cumulative amount of levies outstanding at 31 December 2024' = EUR 26,286,504 (EUR 26.3m) [spreadsheet total row, last column]; Irish Examiner (16 Jun 2026) 'Some EUR 26m in levies imposed in 2024 were never collected'; a Dáil quotation of 'more than EUR 30m already owed' by Mary Lou McDonald is relayed there. No source for EUR 42m found (possibly a 2025 year-end figure not yet published, or a different measure). Do NOT carry EUR 42m; if needed say 'about EUR 26 million at end-2024 (Department of Housing return)'.

(10) 'Revenue have announced that they will not be collecting these outstanding levies as part of the new Derelict Property Tax': VERIFIED B only via press: Irish Examiner 16 Jun 2026: 'It has now been confirmed that outstanding levies owed to councils will not be transferred to Revenue for collection. Revenue will only be responsible for collecting tax accrued from January 2027 onwards.' and 'Government sources stressed that local authorities can continue to chase property owners for unpaid levies' [f3_irishexaminer_revenue_wont_collect.txt]. Budget 2027 tax chapter could not be read (403); no Revenue statement located.

(11) 'Revenue have a 95% collection rate for the Local Property Tax': CLOSE, wording differs. Revenue's published LPT 'payment compliance' is 96.63% for LPT 2024 [f3_revenue_pt_stats_300725.txt, grep '96.63%'; 'Return compliance' 97%] and 96.29% (payment) / 86% (return) for LPT 2026 as of the Aug 2026 release [f3_revenue_pt_stats_050826.txt, grep '96.29%']. These are compliance indicators (properties with returns/payments or arrangements up to date), not a 'collection rate' of money.

(12) 'Vacant Homes Tax: 3,932 properties paying in 2023': VERIFIED A. Revenue 'Chargeable Period 1: 1 Nov 22 - 31 Oct 23, As at 01/07/25': 6,716 declared vacant; 3,932 liable; 2,784 exempt; total liability EUR 2.37m [f3_revenue_pt_stats_300725.txt]. (An earlier Department of Finance figure of 3,942 liable appears in search snippets only; not fetched, do not use.) 'Liable' is not 'paying'.

(13) 'shrunk to 1,454 in 2025': VERIFIED A but STALE. 'Chargeable Period 3: 1 Nov 24 - 31 Oct 25, As of 10/03/26': 1,998 declared vacant; 1,454 liable; 544 exempt; liability EUR 2m [f3_revenue_pt_stats_200326.txt]. The newer Revenue release (As of 23/06/26): 2,193 declared; 1,655 liable; 538 exempt; EUR 2m [f3_revenue_pt_stats_050826.txt]. So use 1,655 if the page cites the latest provisional figure ('returns are open to amendment ... provisional'). Rate context: period 1 rate three times base LPT; period 3 seven times base LPT [f3_revenue_pt_stats_050826.txt]. Period 2 (1 Nov 23-31 Oct 24) is not in the three saved releases.

(14) '1.8% of the 79,703 vacant homes identified by Geodirectory paid the VHT last year': COMPUTATION OK (1,454/79,703 = 1.82%) but the denominator is the Q4 2025 (December 2025) GeoDirectory count '79,703 residential units were classified as vacant by GeoDirectory in December 2025' [f3_geodir_q4_2025_news.txt]; the Q2 2025 count was 80,328 [f3_geodir_q2_2025_news.txt]. Not a compliance rate: GeoDirectory 'vacant' is a stock-share measure (vacant addresses as share of residential stock, EXCLUDING derelicts and buildings under construction) whereas VHT applies only to residential properties used as a dwelling for fewer than 30 days in the chargeable period and 'will not apply if the property is derelict or uninhabitable, was sold in the chargeable period, is subject to a qualifying tenancy, or is exempt from LPT' plus return-based exemptions [f3_revenue_pt_stats_050826.txt VHT text]. The C&AG-reported range of potential vacant homes is 57,000 to 81,000 'depending on the data source' [f3_rte_caag_vht.txt].

(15) C&AG 'lenient approach' and 'normal practice': PARTLY VERIFIED B. RTE: 'The report said the Revenue has adopted a "lenient approach" because the tax was in a start-up phase and did not apply late filing surcharges'; low declaration rate; high use of exemptions; of 44 sampled returns 55% filed late and 63% of late filers paid late; recommends a register built from ESB Networks, local authority and GeoDirectory data; Secretary General John Hogan confirmed a derelict property tax in this year's Finance Bill [f3_rte_caag_vht.txt, published 30 Sep 2026]. The phrase 'is normal practice when new taxes are introduced' was not found in any saved source; the C&AG report itself was not located.

(16) Derelict Property Tax facts: Budget 2026 (Oct 2025) announced it: 'A new Derelict Property Tax (DPT) has been announced in Budget 2026 ... collected by the Revenue Commissioners and will replace the current Derelict Sites Levy'; to be legislated in Finance Bill 2026; local authorities to identify properties in 2026; 'preliminary register ... in 2027'; 'The rate of the DPT is yet to be determined; however, it is envisaged that the tax rate would not be lower than the current 7% rate'; the replacement was a May 2022 recommendation of the Joint Committee on Housing, Local Government and Heritage [f3_budget2026_tax_policy_changes.txt ch.10, p.17-18; grep 'Derelict Property Tax']. Budget 2027 (6 Oct 2026): Minister Harris: 'Legislation to provide for this is now being included in this year's Finance Bill ... preliminary registers of dereliction will be published on 1 September 2027. The rate of tax will be 7 per cent and Revenue will use its full range of powers' [f3_harris_budget2027_statement.txt]. So the DPT was ANNOUNCED in Budget 2026 and DETAILED in Budget 2027; the essay's 'Budget 2027 measure' and 'last week's budget announcement' refer to the detail. Secondary (Tier 2, law-firm) only: 7% of 'self-assessed value'; phased - towns/cities of 4,000+ population from 2027 (107 towns), 2,000+ from 2028 (171 towns); preliminary registers 1 Sep 2027, final 1 Mar 2028; first filing and payment deadline 23 June 2028 [f3_kpmg_budget2027_property.txt; f3_arthurcox_budget2027.txt: 'first pay and file period ... 1 March 2028 to 23 June 2028']. This corroborates the essay's 'first payment won't be till June 2028'. The essay's 'fully enforced only after 2031' and '40 years of ineffective penalties' are the authors' extrapolation.

(17) Unverified/unsourced in essay: 'council executives publicly announced that "there are few mechanisms to force owners to pay and the collection of DSLs can often be a waiting game"' (no source given; not found); 'Fine Gael promised a 10% tax on derelict sites ... 1983-1986 Joint Programme for Government' and the 1986 quotation (no primary found); CIF/Grand Canal homes and 'EUR 16 million' sale valuation (not checked); authors' testimony 'in 2021 and last year': 2021 CONFIRMED (Anois opening statement to the Joint Committee, 14 Dec 2021, saved, in which they ask for Revenue to collect the 7% levy and a vacancy tax: 'We propose Inland Revenue collect the 7% annual levy'), 2025 hearing not located.

SUGGESTED SENTENCES FOR places/ireland.md (primary-backed): 'The Derelict Sites Act 1990 lets local authorities enter derelict urban land on a register and charge the owner an annual levy on its market value - 3 per cent initially, raised to 7 per cent for local financial years from 2020 by the Planning and Development (Amendment) Act 2018.' 'At the end of 2024 the registers held 2,140 sites; in 2024 councils levied 778 sites for EUR 8.6 million, received EUR 0.82 million of that, and had EUR 26.3 million of levies outstanding; nine of 31 authorities levied no site (Department of Housing return).' 'Budget 2026 announced a Derelict Property Tax collected by Revenue to replace the levy; Budget 2027 set the rate at 7 per cent with preliminary registers due on 1 September 2027.' 'Ireland also levies a Vacant Homes Tax (self-assessed, since 2022): Revenue's provisional figures show 3,932 liable properties for the first chargeable period and 1,655 for the third, at seven times the base LPT rate; a Comptroller and Auditor General report (September 2026) found limited effect.' And, attributed: 'Campaigners at #DerelictIreland argue that the registers capture a small fraction of the roughly 19,800 derelict residential buildings GeoDirectory counted in mid-2025.'

uncertainties: The 2025 Oireachtas hearing and the Budget 2027 Tax Policy Changes PDF (rate basis 'self-assessed value', phase-in, deadlines) could not be read; DPT mechanics beyond Harris's statement rest on KPMG/Arthur Cox summaries (Tier 2) until the Finance (No. 2) Bill 2026 text or the Department PDF is read. Part 2 of the essay (due 22 Oct 2026) is expected to cover design and is where 'designed to fail' is argued; today's Part 1 mostly covers the levy.

EUR 42m has no support; primary is EUR 26.3m (end-2024). The authors' '10 councils' is 9 in the primary. The 1,454 VHT figure is superseded by 1,655. The 79,703 vacancy denominator is Dec 2025, not Q2 2025 (80,328). Any of these appearing on the wiki unreconciled would be an error against the primary.

The levy/tax is status-based (derelict) and levied on market value of 'urban land' registered; it is not a land value tax and the essay does not argue Georgist LVT. Ireland-page framing must not overclaim a Georgist link; the connection is the holding-cost/idle-land logic and the failure-of-enforcement lesson.
The authors' interpretation of write-offs as failure conflicts with Cork City's own breakdown (79% of write-offs because dereliction was removed or council acquired the site).
TheJournal.ie page is an opinion/essay ('The Housing Essay'); the 'Comments Summary AI-GENERATED' box on the page is not content.
Possible overlap with future queue items: Part 2 of this essay; the Finance Bill 2026 text; the C&AG report. T1 should dedup by URL.

The 'Finance Act 2025/Budget 2026' pointer in the task brief was only half right: the tax was announced in Budget 2026 (Oct 2025, Department of Finance Tax Policy Changes ch.10) and legislated in Finance (No. 2) Bill 2026 (per Forvis Mazars via search, not fetched).
